faq.a: To rule out vesicoureteric reflux, which changes surgical planning.
faq.q: Why is a VCUG performed if ultrasound already shows obstruction?

faq.a: Mild cases (SFU grade I–II) may improve; close monitoring is required.
Open ureteric reimplantation is reliable and does not need advanced endoscopic equipment.
faq.q: What is the preferred surgical technique in low‑resource settings?

exam: A 3‑month‑old infant has prenatal hydronephrosis; ultrasound now shows grade III hydronephrosis with a dilated ureter. What is your next step? — Order VCUG to exclude reflux, then plan diuretic renography to assess function.

A child presents with recurrent febrile UTIs and ultrasound shows a dilated distal ureter. How do you differentiate UVJO from VUR? — Perform VCUG; reflux will be seen in VUR, while UVJO shows a tapered distal ureter without reflux.
During surgery for UVJO, why might you place a ureteric stent post‑reimplantation? — To maintain drainage while the anastomosis heals and prevent obstruction from edema.
What clinical sign suggests worsening obstruction in a child with known UVJO? — New onset flank pain with vomiting or a rapid increase in hydronephrosis on repeat ultrasound.
Why is diuretic renography preferred over plain ultrasound for deciding surgery? — It quantifies split renal function and drainage time, identifying kidneys that are functionally compromised.
In a low‑resource hospital without renography, how would you decide on surgery? — Use serial ultrasounds showing progressive dilation and clinical deterioration (pain, infection, rising creatinine).
What are the long‑term risks if UVJO is left untreated? — Chronic renal scarring, hypertension, and possible end‑stage renal disease.
Why is NSAID use discouraged in a child with acute UVJO? — NSAIDs reduce renal prostaglandin‑mediated blood flow, worsening renal perfusion in an obstructed kidney.
ai.title: Ureterovesical Junction Obstruction in Children
ai.subject: Paediatrics
ai.summary: Ureterovesical junction obstruction (UVJO) is a congenital blockage at the distal ureter causing hydronephrosis. It is the commonest cause of pediatric urinary tract dilation and must be recognised early for renal preservation.

b: Diagnosed by ultrasound showing a dilated ureter (hydroureter) and renal pelvis with a normal ureteropelvic junction.
VCUG may demonstrate a tapered distal ureter and exclude reflux.
sections.p: UVJO is a functional or anatomic narrowing at the ureter’s entry into the bladder, leading to upstream dilatation of the ureter and renal pelvis.

b: Grade I–II often managed conservatively.
Grade III–IV usually need surgical intervention.
sections.p: Severity is graded by the Society for Fetal Urology (SFU) hydronephrosis scale on ultrasound, from grade I (mild) to grade IV (severe cortical thinning).

b: Congenital muscular dysplasia of distal ureter (most common).
Extrinsic compression by pelvic masses (e.g., ovarian cysts, neuroblastoma).
Post‑infectious scarring (rare in low‑resource settings).
sections.p: Most UVJO are congenital due to abnormal smooth‑muscle development; secondary causes are rare.

b: Prenatal hydronephrosis on routine scan.
Recurrent urinary tract infection.
Intermittent abdominal or flank pain, especially after fluids.
Palpable abdominal mass in severe cases.
sections.p: Infants may be asymptomatic; older children present with urinary symptoms or flank pain.
If a test is unavailable (e.g., diuretic renography), rely on serial ultrasounds and clinical course to decide on surgery.

t.b: Is there hydronephrosis and hydroureter? – Shows dilated pelvis and ureter; severity grading guides management.
Is vesicoureteric reflux present? – Excludes reflux; a normal study supports primary UVJO.
Is renal function impaired and is drainage obstructive? – Split function <40 % or delayed T½ >20 min suggests surgery.
Is renal function preserved? – Normal values reassure; rising creatinine signals urgent intervention.
Is infection present? – Positive culture prompts antibiotics before any invasive procedure.

b: Rapidly worsening hydronephrosis on serial scans.
Declining renal function (creatinine rise).
Recurrent febrile UTI.
Hypertension secondary to renal scarring.
sections.p: Unrecognised obstruction can lead to irreversible renal damage.

b: Antibiotics for UTI (e.g., amoxicillin‑clavulanate) before any procedure.
Endoscopic balloon dilatation or laser incision for short strictures.
Ureteric reimplantation (Cohen or Politano‑Leadbetter) for long‑segment obstruction.
Post‑op stent placement for 4–6 weeks to ensure drainage.
Avoid nephrotoxic drugs (e.g., NSAIDs) during acute obstruction.
sections.p: Treat infection first, then relieve obstruction surgically while preserving renal tissue.

b: Ultrasound at 3 months, then 6 months, then annually.
Renography if renal function <40 % or hydronephrosis persists.
Educate families on early signs of UTI.
sections.p: Long‑term monitoring prevents late renal loss.

b: Ureteropelvic junction obstruction – presents with a normal distal ureter and a dilated renal pelvis only.
Vesicoureteric reflux – shows reflux on VCUG and may have scarred kidney rather than a tapered distal ureter.
Mild hydronephrosis on a single ultrasound may be transient; serial imaging is essential.
Normal serum creatinine can mask unilateral loss; split function studies are needed.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden increase in abdominal/flank pain with vomiting
Fever with dysuria or flank tenderness
